title: The Speed Dividend: What AI Is Quietly Doing to Marketing and Creative Agency Margins
excerpt: A website brief that used to take six hours now takes two, because of AI. The deliverable hasn't changed. For agencies still billing by the hour, that saved time has quietly disappeared from the invoice.
content:
A website brief that used to take a Brisbane copywriter six hours now takes two, because the first draft comes from an AI tool and the remaining four hours go into editing, tone and strategy rather than generation. The deliverable is the same. The time behind it has quietly halved. For an agency still pricing on an hourly rate card, that is not a productivity win sitting on the P&L. It is four hours of fee that simply stopped existing.

Every marketing, creative and media agency built its pricing on a simple assumption: time spent and value delivered move together. AI tools have not broken that assumption everywhere, but they have broken it in enough of the work, research, first drafts, image variations, basic edits, that the gap between the two is now wide enough to matter. The work clients are paying for still gets delivered. The hours it used to take to deliver it do not.

Most agencies have not repriced anything yet. The scope documents and rate cards written eighteen months ago are still the ones being quoted today, which means the speed gained from new tools is, by default, a gift to the client rather than a margin recovered by the business that built the capability to deliver it.

The Billable Hour Was Built on an Assumption That Is Now Wrong in Places

Not every task has compressed. Strategy, client relationships, creative direction and the judgement calls that separate a good campaign from an average one still take the time they always have, arguably more of it, because reviewing and correcting AI-assisted output is its own skill. The compression sits mainly in the production layer: first drafts, social content variations, basic layout work, transcription, research summaries. An agency that bills everything at the same hourly rate, regardless of which layer the hour sits in, is quietly averaging away the problem rather than solving it.

A content team producing a month of social variations used to budget a full day for the first draft round. If a tool now produces a usable first pass in under an hour, the remaining time is refinement, not generation, and it is worth a different rate, or a different kind of fee altogether, to reflect that.

Where the Speed Dividend Actually Goes

In our experience, the time an agency saves through AI tools goes one of three places. It becomes unbilled capacity that quietly shows up as spare hours nobody tracks, and nobody notices until utilisation reporting looks oddly soft for a team that still seems busy. It becomes extra scope absorbed into the same fee because nobody wants an awkward conversation with the client about why the invoice looks the same for less visible work. Or, less often, it becomes genuine margin recovered because the agency repriced deliberately rather than by accident. Only the third outcome actually benefits the business that invested in the tools in the first place.

Repricing Without Pretending AI Never Happened

The fix is not to hide the efficiency gain or to apologise for it. Clients increasingly expect agencies to use these tools, and most would rather pay for a strong outcome than for a specific number of hours. Shifting part of the fee structure toward deliverables, retainers scoped to outcomes, or a blended rate that reflects where the real time now sits, is the kind of change a pricing reset is built to work through properly, rather than guessing at a new rate card overnight.

That usually means separating the rate card into layers rather than rewriting it from scratch. Strategic and client-facing hours can often stay priced as they are. Production hours, the ones most affected by new tools, move toward a fixed fee per deliverable or a package price, so the agency is paid for the asset produced rather than for however long it happened to take that week.

Agencies in Brisbane, Sydney and Melbourne are all working through versions of this at the same time, which means the businesses that reprice deliberately over the next year will set the market rather than follow it. The agencies still billing exactly as they did last year will find their margin has quietly moved without anyone deciding it should.

None of this is a reason to abandon the billable hour altogether, but it is a reason to look at where the hours actually go before the rate card quietly goes out of date. That kind of margin visibility, understanding which parts of the business are earning what they used to and which are not, is exactly the sort of question that benefits from an outside, numbers-first perspective rather than another internal debate about rates.

faqs.q: Should a marketing agency still bill by the hour when AI speeds up delivery?
faqs.a: Hourly billing still works for the parts of the job that have not sped up, strategy, client management and creative direction. It breaks down for production tasks where AI has genuinely cut the time in half or more. Most agencies are better served by splitting the fee structure rather than keeping one blended hourly rate across work that behaves completely differently now.

faqs.q: How can a creative agency reprice its services as AI reduces delivery time?
faqs.a: Start by separating which deliverables have genuinely compressed from which have not, then move the compressed ones toward a deliverable or outcome-based fee rather than an hourly one. A structured pricing reset works through this properly, using actual job data rather than guesswork, so the new rate card reflects where time is really being spent now.

faqs.q: Is the billable hour model becoming obsolete for agencies using AI tools?
faqs.a: Not obsolete, but incomplete on its own. The billable hour still fits strategic and judgement-heavy work reasonably well. It fits production work poorly once a tool can do in minutes what used to take hours. Most agencies will end up running a blended model rather than abandoning hourly billing altogether.

faqs.q: What is value-based pricing and does it work for marketing and creative agencies?
faqs.a: Value-based pricing charges for the outcome or deliverable rather than the hours behind it. It suits agency work reasonably well because clients are usually buying a campaign result, a brand asset or a finished piece of content, not a specific number of hours, which makes it easier to hold the fee steady even as delivery gets faster.

faqs.q: How do I know if AI efficiency is already eroding my agency's margin?
faqs.a: Compare the time a job actually took against the time it was quoted or budgeted for, job by job, over the last few months. If delivery time has been quietly dropping while fees have stayed flat, the margin gain from that efficiency is going somewhere, usually to the client by default rather than to the business.

faqs.q: What does a pricing reset for a marketing or creative agency typically cost?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the size of the service offering being reviewed, from a handful of core retainer packages through to a full agency rate card covering every service line. Current engagement pricing is set out on the pricing page, and most agencies start with their highest-volume service lines before deciding whether to extend the review further.
